claims.text: Initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles form a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles contain elemental clusters.
The Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles exhibit elemental surface segregation, particularly at low-coordination sites.
Local chemical heterogeneity governs the onset of premelting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles.
Local chemical heterogeneity governs the spatial progression of premelting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles.
Chemical complexity creates locally weakly bonded regions in the HEA nanoparticles.
Weakly bonded regions initiate premelting at segregated clusters or at the nanoparticle surface.
Premelting initiated at heterogeneous sites produces a progressive, multi-step melting process.
Comparable homogeneous single-metal nanoparticles melt more uniformly and abruptly than the HEA nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit an extended premelting regime.
Localized molten regions in the HEA nanoparticles will coalesce before complete melting.
The complete melting transition of the HEA nanoparticles will occur at a higher overall temperature than that of the matched single-metal baseline.
Kinetic arrest during rapid thermal processing can preserve non-equilibrium solid-solution states in multielement nanoparticles.
The temperature span and spatial distribution of premelting can vary with synthesis details and nanoparticle dimensions.
Absence of localized or multi-step melting in the HEA relative to the matched single-metal control would refute the proposed mechanism.
